title: Binary search with no end in sight
hook: Binary search starts from both ends. What if the list has no end you can see?

knows: binary search halves a sorted list that has a known length (binary-search)
doesNotKnow: that a sorted list of unknown length can be binary-searched by doubling a probe first

misconception: Binary search needs to know where the list ends; with no end you must scan one by one.
objective: The learner can explain that probing positions 1, 2, 4, ... finds a gap holding the target in about log2(position) steps and halving that gap costs about as many again, so a target at position 1000 takes 17 comparisons instead of a 1,001-step scan.

claims.text: With the target at position 1000, probing positions 1, 2, 4, ... takes 11 comparisons (the 11th probe, at 1024, passes the target), leaving the gap 513-1023; 6 halvings find it, 17 comparisons in all.
claims.source: Demo.tsx FULL, computed with the same doubleOnce/halveOnce rules the stage uses; builder re-ran the count in Node (2026-10-14). Counting rule: every comparison of the target with a list value counts once; doubling starts at position 1 (position 0 is not probed) and the halving searches the open gap strictly between the last two probes (binary probes 768, 896, 960, 992, 1008, 1000). NOTE: the brief says 18; that count also probes position 0 first and searches the closed gap 512-1024 (builder reproduced 18 with that convention). The prediction's answer 'About 20' holds under either. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own node mirror of doubleOnce/halveOnce (fc21/dbl.mjs): 11 doubling probes to 1024, gap 513-1023, halvings 768, 896, 960, 992, 1008, 1000, total 17. Reveal reads these from FULL. The brief's 18 is a different counting convention, as noted.

claims.text: A scan from the start needs 1,001 comparisons to reach position 1000.
claims.source: Positions 0 through 1000 are 1,001 positions, one comparison each. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Positions 0..1000 = 1,001 comparisons; Demo SCAN = POS + 1.

claims.text: Because the list is sorted, a probe whose value is smaller than the target means the target lies further right, and the first probe that passes it bounds the target between the last two probes.
claims.source: Sortedness: value(i) < target implies the target's position is > i; value(2^k) > target and value(2^(k-1)) < target bound it to (2^(k-1), 2^k). The stage list is value(i) = 3i + 7 (target 3007), shown only through the probed values. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Sortedness argument; value(i) = 3i + 7 is strictly increasing.

claims.text: Doubling reaches a gap holding the target after about log2(position) probes (the number of doublings it takes). That gap is about as wide as the last jump, so halving it can need nearly as many probes again, and the cost grows like twice log2 of the position.
claims.source: Derivation: k = ceil(log2 p) + 1 doubling probes; the gap has 2^(k-2) - 1 positions, so binary search adds at most k - 2. Bentley and Yao (1976), 'An almost optimal algorithm for unbounded searching', Information Processing Letters 5(3) (citation from the brief, written from memory: check before verifying). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Derivation re-run: for every target position 2..65,536 the count is at most 2 ceil(log2(p+1)) + 1. Bentley & Yao (1976), 'An almost optimal algorithm for unbounded searching', IPL 5(3):82-87, bibliographic details confirmed via web search (Wikipedia 'Exponential search', XJTU scholar listing); full text not opened, the sentence rests on the derivation. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): reveal reworded: 'costs about as many again' became 'can need nearly as many again', pointing at the stage gap label; log2 glossed as the number of doublings.

claims.text: For a target at position one million the same method takes 34 comparisons.
claims.source: Builder's Node run of the same counting rule as c1 (2026-10-14): position 1,000,000 -> 34; position 4,000 -> 19 (used in recall). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own run: position 1,000,000 gives 21 doubling + 13 halving = 34; position 4,000 gives 19.

claims.text: The gap 513-1023 is 511 positions wide, and halving it can take up to 9 comparisons; this target (position 1000) sat on an early midpoint and took 6. (Stage label: 'gap 513–1023: 511 wide, up to 9 halvings'.)
claims.source: Binary search with a 3-way compare on w positions needs at most floor(log2 w) + 1 probes: floor(log2 511) + 1 = 8 + 1 = 9. Midpoints for 1000 in 513..1023: 768, 896, 960, 992, 1008, 1000 = 6 (Demo.tsx halveOnce(), maxHalves()). | Added 2026-10-14 (v2) by demo-builder.

recall.question: A sorted list of unknown length holds your item at about position 4,000. Doubling a probe, then halving the last gap, takes about how many comparisons?
recall.why: 13 doubling probes (1 up to 4,096) find the gap, and halving it adds 6: 19 comparisons with the lesson's counting.
